questions.stem: An experiment using a spirit burner gives an enthalpy of combustion value that is lower than the literature value. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Too much fuel was burned in the experiment
Heat was lost to the surroundings during the experiment
The water was too hot at the start

questions.explanation: The most common source of error in calorimetry experiments is heat loss to the surroundings. Not all the heat from combustion goes into the water; some is lost to the air, the container, and by evaporation. This means the measured temperature rise is smaller than it should be, giving a lower calculated enthalpy value.

questions.stem: When calculating enthalpy change per mole from calorimetry data, after finding Q using Q = mcΔT, what is the next step?

options.text: Multiply Q by the number of moles
Divide Q by the mass of water used
Divide Q by the number of moles of reactant and add the correct sign
Multiply Q by the specific heat capacity

questions.explanation: After calculating Q (energy transferred in joules), you convert to kJ by dividing by 1000, then divide by the number of moles of the reactant to get kJ/mol. If the temperature increased, ΔH is negative (exothermic); if it decreased, ΔH is positive (endothermic).
